back:
Adrenergic agonist; non-selective α1/α2/β1/β2 agonist
Key parameters: catecholamine; direct-acting sympathomimetic; first-line in anaphylaxis; increases HR/contractility and bronchodilates; short acting.

Adrenergic agonist; mainly α1/α2 + β1 agonist
Key parameters: catecholamine; direct-acting sympathomimetic; strong vasoconstrictor; used in shock/hypotension; little β2 effect.

β2-adrenergic agonist; short-acting β2 agonist (SABA)
Key parameters: bronchodilator; used as asthma/COPD reliever; adverse effects: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia.

β1-adrenergic agonist; positive inotrope
Key parameters: direct sympathomimetic; β1 > β2/α1; used in acute heart failure/cardiogenic shock; increases contractility.

α1-adrenergic blocker
Key parameters: selective α1 antagonist; vasodilator; used in hypertension/BPH; adverse effect: first-dose orthostatic hypotension.

β-blocker; non-selective β1/β2 antagonist
Key parameters: lipophilic; no β1 selectivity; avoid in asthma/COPD; uses include hypertension, angina, tremor, migraine prophylaxis.

β-blocker; β1-selective antagonist
Key parameters: cardioselective at usual doses; used in hypertension, angina, chronic heart failure, arrhythmias; may lose selectivity at high doses.

β-blocker; β1-selective antagonist
Key parameters: cardioselective; commonly used in chronic heart failure and hypertension; reduces HR, contractility, renin.

β-blocker; non-selective β + α1 antagonist
Key parameters: vasodilating beta-blocker; useful in chronic heart failure; blocks β1/β2 and α1.

β-blocker; β1-selective with NO-mediated vasodilation
Key parameters: cardioselective; vasodilating; used in hypertension/heart failure in some settings.

Parasympatholytic/antimuscarinic; tertiary amine
Key parameters: crosses CNS/BBB; non-selective muscarinic antagonist; used in bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning; causes dry mouth, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention.

Parasympatholytic/antimuscarinic; tertiary amine
Key parameters: crosses BBB; prominent CNS effects; used for motion sickness; sedating/amnesic.

Parasympatholytic/antimuscarinic; quaternary ammonium compound
Key parameters: poor CNS penetration; inhaled bronchodilator; short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA); used in COPD/asthma.

Parasympatholytic/antimuscarinic; quaternary ammonium compound
Key parameters: inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA); COPD maintenance; poor CNS penetration.

Indirect parasympathomimetic; reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; quaternary ammonium
Key parameters: poor CNS penetration; used in myasthenia gravis, reversal of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade, ileus/urinary retention.

Indirect parasympathomimetic; reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; tertiary amine
Key parameters: crosses BBB; used for severe antimuscarinic toxicity; more CNS activity than neostigmine.

Acetylcholinesterase reactivator/antidote
Key parameters: used with atropine in organophosphate poisoning; works best before enzyme aging; restores nicotinic and muscarinic transmission.

ACE inhibitor; antihypertensive/heart failure drug
Key parameters: blocks angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdown; adverse effects: cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema; contraindicated in pregnancy.

ACE inhibitor; antihypertensive/heart failure drug
Key parameters: similar to enalapril; renal/cardioprotective in appropriate patients; cough/hyperkalemia/angioedema risk.

Angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB)
Key parameters: AT1 receptor antagonist; no bradykinin cough usually; adverse effect: hyperkalemia; contraindicated in pregnancy.

Angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB)
Key parameters: AT1 blocker; used in hypertension/heart failure; hyperkalemia risk; pregnancy contraindication.

Calcium channel blocker; dihydropyridine CCB
Key parameters: vascular selective; antihypertensive/antianginal; adverse effects: ankle edema, flushing, headache.

Calcium channel blocker; non-dihydropyridine CCB
Key parameters: cardiac selective; decreases AV conduction and contractility; used for rate control/angina; adverse effects: constipation, bradycardia, AV block.

Calcium channel blocker; non-dihydropyridine CCB
Key parameters: cardiac and vascular effects; slows AV node; used for angina/rate control; less constipation than verapamil.

Loop diuretic
Key parameters: inhibits Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter in thick ascending limb; strong diuresis; adverse effects: hypokalemia, ototoxicity, dehydration.

Thiazide diuretic
Key parameters: inhibits Na+/Cl− cotransporter in distal convoluted tubule; hypertension; adverse effects: hypokalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia.

Potassium-sparing diuretic; aldosterone receptor antagonist
Key parameters: used in heart failure/hyperaldosteronism; adverse effects: hyperkalemia, gynecomastia, menstrual effects.

Organic nitrate; antianginal vasodilator
Key parameters: releases NO; venodilation reduces preload; acute angina relief; adverse effects: headache, hypotension, tolerance; contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.

Cardiac glycoside; positive inotrope
Key parameters: inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase; increases vagal tone and contractility; narrow therapeutic index; toxicity includes arrhythmias, GI symptoms, visual disturbances.

Antiarrhythmic; class III potassium-channel blocker mainly
Key parameters: broad antiarrhythmic actions; used for AF and ventricular arrhythmias; toxicities: thyroid, pulmonary fibrosis, liver, corneal deposits, photosensitivity.

Antiarrhythmic class Ib; local anesthetic
Key parameters: sodium-channel blocker; ventricular arrhythmias especially ischemia-related; also local anesthetic; CNS toxicity possible.

Parenteral anticoagulant; indirect thrombin/Xa inhibitor via antithrombin
Key parameters: rapid onset; monitored by aPTT for unfractionated heparin; antidote: protamine; risk HIT and bleeding.

Oral anticoagulant; vitamin K antagonist
Key parameters: inhibits factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S; monitored by INR; many interactions; teratogenic; antidote: vitamin K/PCC.

Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC); factor Xa inhibitor
Key parameters: oral; fixed dosing in many uses; no routine INR; bleeding risk; reversal may use andexanet alfa where available.

Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC); factor Xa inhibitor
Key parameters: oral factor Xa inhibitor; used for AF/VTE; no routine INR; bleeding risk.

Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC); direct thrombin inhibitor
Key parameters: oral; antidote: idarucizumab; bleeding and dyspepsia risk; renal elimination important.

Antiplatelet NSAID; irreversible COX inhibitor
Key parameters: inhibits TXA2 in platelets; antiaggregant at low dose; adverse effects: GI bleeding, bronchospasm, Reye risk in children.

Antiplatelet drug; P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist
Key parameters: prodrug; prevents platelet aggregation; used after ACS/stents; bleeding risk.

Fibrinolytic/thrombolytic; recombinant tPA
Key parameters: converts plasminogen to plasmin; used in selected ischemic stroke/MI/PE; major risk: bleeding/intracranial hemorrhage.

Hypolipidemic; HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor/statin
Key parameters: lowers LDL; plaque stabilization; adverse effects: myopathy, ↑ liver enzymes; avoid in pregnancy.

Hypolipidemic; HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor/statin
Key parameters: LDL-lowering statin; CYP interactions important; myopathy risk.

Benzodiazepine; positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A
Key parameters: long acting; anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant; overdose antidote: flumazenil; respiratory depression risk with alcohol/opioids.

Benzodiazepine; GABA-A positive allosteric modulator
Key parameters: intermediate acting; useful in status epilepticus and severe anxiety; no active oxidative metabolites; flumazenil reverses overdose.

Benzodiazepine; GABA-A positive allosteric modulator
Key parameters: short acting; procedural sedation/anesthesia induction; anterograde amnesia; respiratory depression risk.

Barbiturate; GABA-A enhancer
Key parameters: anticonvulsant; longer duration; overdose causes CNS/respiratory depression; no specific antagonist.

Non-benzodiazepine hypnotic; Z-drug
Key parameters: acts at GABA-A benzodiazepine site, relatively BZ1 selective; insomnia; less anticonvulsant/muscle relaxant effect.

Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist; antidote
Key parameters: reverses benzodiazepines/Z-drugs; can trigger seizures in dependence or mixed overdose.

Antidepressant; SSRI
Key parameters: increases serotonin by reuptake inhibition; long half-life; adverse effects: sexual dysfunction, GI upset, serotonin syndrome risk.

Antidepressant; SSRI
Key parameters: first-line depression/anxiety; serotonergic adverse effects; fewer dangerous overdoses than TCAs.

Antidepressant; tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), tertiary amine
Key parameters: inhibits 5-HT/NE reuptake; strong anticholinergic, sedating; overdose causes arrhythmias/seizures; used also for neuropathic pain.

Antidepressant; tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), tertiary amine
Key parameters: 5-HT/NE reuptake inhibition; anticholinergic/cardiotoxic in overdose.

Antipsychotic; typical high-potency D2 antagonist
Key parameters: strong extrapyramidal symptom risk; low anticholinergic/sedative burden; used in acute psychosis/agitation.

Antipsychotic; typical low-potency D2 antagonist
Key parameters: more sedation, anticholinergic effects, hypotension; lower EPS than high-potency typicals.

Antipsychotic; atypical
Key parameters: treatment-resistant schizophrenia; adverse effects: agranulocytosis, myocarditis, seizures, weight gain; requires blood monitoring.

Antipsychotic; atypical D2/5-HT2 antagonist
Key parameters: can raise prolactin; EPS at higher doses; used in schizophrenia/bipolar/irritability.

Mood stabilizer
Key parameters: bipolar disorder; narrow therapeutic index; toxicity: tremor, nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism; renal monitoring; teratogenic risk.

Antiepileptic/mood stabilizer
Key parameters: increases GABA and blocks Na+ channels; broad-spectrum; adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, neural tube defects.

Antiepileptic; sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: focal seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar; adverse effects: agranulocytosis, hyponatremia, CYP induction, teratogenicity.

Antiepileptic/mood stabilizer; sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: focal/generalized seizures, bipolar depression; serious rash/Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk.

Antiepileptic; SV2A modulator
Key parameters: broad use; few interactions; adverse effects: irritability, mood changes.

Antiepileptic; sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: focal/tonic-clonic seizures; nonlinear kinetics; adverse effects: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, ataxia, teratogenicity.

Opioid analgesic; full μ-opioid receptor agonist
Key parameters: strong analgesic; adverse effects: respiratory depression, constipation, miosis, dependence; overdose antidote: naloxone.

Opioid analgesic; full μ-opioid receptor agonist
Key parameters: very potent, lipophilic; anesthesia/severe pain; respiratory depression; naloxone reverses.

Opioid analgesic/antitussive; weak μ agonist prodrug
Key parameters: converted by CYP2D6 to morphine; variable response; constipation/sedation; avoid in some children.

Opioid-like analgesic; weak μ agonist + 5-HT/NE reuptake inhibition
Key parameters: seizure and serotonin syndrome risk; dependence possible.

Opioid receptor antagonist; antidote
Key parameters: reverses opioid overdose/respiratory depression; short duration; may precipitate withdrawal.

NSAID; reversible non-selective COX inhibitor
Key parameters: analgesic/antipyretic/anti-inflammatory; adverse effects: GI bleeding, renal injury, bronchospasm risk.

NSAID; COX inhibitor
Key parameters: potent anti-inflammatory/analgesic; higher cardiovascular risk than some NSAIDs; GI/renal toxicity.

Analgesic/antipyretic; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory effect
Key parameters: overdose causes hepatic necrosis; antidote: N-acetylcysteine; generally no platelet/GI COX effects like NSAIDs.

Antidote/mucolytic
Key parameters: replenishes glutathione; used in paracetamol poisoning; also breaks mucus disulfide bonds.

Intravenous general anesthetic
Key parameters: rapid induction/recovery; GABA-A potentiation; adverse effects: hypotension, respiratory depression; antiemetic.

Intravenous anesthetic; NMDA receptor antagonist
Key parameters: dissociative anesthesia; preserves airway reflexes more than many anesthetics; increases BP/HR; emergence reactions.

Inhaled general anesthetic
Key parameters: volatile anesthetic; rapid induction/recovery; relatively non-irritating; malignant hyperthermia risk with susceptible patients.

Local anesthetic; amide type sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: amide local anesthetic; also class Ib antiarrhythmic; systemic toxicity: CNS symptoms, seizures, arrhythmias.

Local anesthetic; amide type sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: long acting; more cardiotoxic than lidocaine; used in regional anesthesia.

Antidote; alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor
Key parameters: used for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning; prevents toxic metabolite formation.

Competitive substrate for alcohol dehydrogenase; antidote alternative
Key parameters: can be used in methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning where fomepizole unavailable; requires monitoring.

β-lactam antibiotic; natural penicillin
Key parameters: cell wall synthesis inhibitor; mainly Gram-positive and spirochetes; β-lactamase sensitive; allergy risk.

β-lactam antibiotic; aminopenicillin/broad-spectrum penicillin
Key parameters: oral; Gram-positive plus some Gram-negative; often combined with clavulanate; rash risk in EBV.

β-lactam antibiotic; antipseudomonal ureidopenicillin
Key parameters: broad spectrum incl. Pseudomonas; often combined with tazobactam; IV severe infections.

β-lactam antibiotic; 1st-generation cephalosporin
Key parameters: Gram-positive coverage, surgical prophylaxis; some Gram-negative; renal elimination.

β-lactam antibiotic; 2nd-generation cephalosporin
Key parameters: more Gram-negative than 1st gen; respiratory infections; β-lactam allergy consideration.

β-lactam antibiotic; 3rd-generation cephalosporin
Key parameters: good Gram-negative and CNS penetration; long half-life; used in meningitis/gonorrhea/sepsis.

β-lactam antibiotic; 4th-generation cephalosporin
Key parameters: broad Gram-negative incl. Pseudomonas plus Gram-positive; severe hospital infections.

Macrolide antibiotic
Key parameters: 50S ribosomal inhibitor; atypical respiratory pathogens; long half-life; QT prolongation risk.

Macrolide antibiotic
Key parameters: 50S inhibitor; CYP3A4 inhibitor; used in respiratory infections and H. pylori regimens; QT risk.

Lincosamide antibiotic
Key parameters: 50S inhibitor; anaerobes and Gram-positive cocci; adverse effect: C. difficile colitis.

Tetracycline antibiotic
Key parameters: 30S inhibitor; atypicals, acne, Lyme, rickettsiae; photosensitivity; avoid in pregnancy/young children.

Aminoglycoside antibiotic
Key parameters: 30S inhibitor; concentration-dependent killing; Gram-negative aerobes; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; requires monitoring.

Fluoroquinolone antibiotic; DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibitor
Key parameters: Gram-negative incl. Pseudomonas; adverse effects: tendinopathy, QT prolongation, CNS effects; avoid pregnancy/children if possible.

Antibiotic/antiprotozoal; DNA-damaging nitroimidazole
Key parameters: anaerobes and protozoa; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; metallic taste.

Antituberculosis drug; mycolic acid synthesis inhibitor
Key parameters: first-line TB; adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy; give pyridoxine/B6.

Antituberculosis drug; RNA polymerase inhibitor
Key parameters: first-line TB; strong CYP inducer; orange body fluids; hepatotoxicity.

Antituberculosis drug
Key parameters: first-line TB; active in acidic phagosomes; adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia.

Antituberculosis drug; arabinosyl transferase inhibitor
Key parameters: first-line TB; adverse effect: optic neuritis/red-green color vision impairment.

Antiviral; guanosine analogue DNA polymerase inhibitor
Key parameters: HSV/VZV; activated by viral thymidine kinase; adverse effect: crystalluria/nephrotoxicity.

Antiviral; neuraminidase inhibitor
Key parameters: influenza A/B; best early; adverse effects: nausea, neuropsychiatric events rarely.

Antifungal; azole, ergosterol synthesis inhibitor
Key parameters: inhibits 14α-demethylase; Candida/Cryptococcus; CYP interactions; hepatotoxicity.

Antifungal; polyene
Key parameters: binds ergosterol and forms pores; severe systemic fungal infections; adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, infusion reactions.

Anthelmintic; microtubule inhibitor
Key parameters: broad helminth coverage; inhibits glucose uptake; adverse effects: GI upset, hepatotoxicity rare.

Anthelmintic; increases parasite membrane Ca2+ permeability
Key parameters: trematodes/cestodes including schistosomiasis; causes spastic paralysis of worms.

H1 antihistamine; second generation
Key parameters: less sedating than first-generation H1 blockers; allergic rhinitis/urticaria; minimal anticholinergic effect.

H1 antihistamine; first generation
Key parameters: sedating; anticholinergic; motion sickness/allergy/insomnia; crosses BBB.

Mast cell stabilizer
Key parameters: prevents mediator release; prophylaxis in allergic disease/asthma; not for acute attack.

Proton pump inhibitor (PPI)
Key parameters: irreversible H+/K+ ATPase inhibitor; peptic ulcer/GERD; CYP interactions; long-term risks include ↓Mg/B12, infections.

Proton pump inhibitor (PPI)
Key parameters: acid suppression; fewer CYP interactions than omeprazole; ulcer/GERD prophylaxis/treatment.

Antiemetic; 5-HT3 receptor antagonist
Key parameters: chemotherapy/postoperative nausea; adverse effects: constipation, QT prolongation.

Antiemetic/prokinetic; D2 antagonist
Key parameters: increases GI motility; adverse effects: extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia.

Antidiarrheal; peripheral μ-opioid receptor agonist
Key parameters: reduces intestinal motility; does not significantly cross BBB at normal doses; avoid in bloody diarrhea/high fever.

Osmotic laxative
Key parameters: constipation and hepatic encephalopathy; traps ammonia in gut; adverse effects: bloating, diarrhea.

IBD anti-inflammatory drug
Key parameters: ulcerative colitis mainly; local anti-inflammatory action in bowel; renal monitoring sometimes needed.

Insulin; short-acting
Key parameters: onset slower than rapid analogues; can be IV in emergencies; hypoglycemia and weight gain risk.

Insulin analogue; rapid-acting
Key parameters: mealtime insulin; fast onset/short duration; hypoglycemia risk.

Insulin analogue; long-acting basal insulin
Key parameters: once daily basal coverage; relatively peakless; hypoglycemia/weight gain risk.

Insulin; intermediate-acting
Key parameters: basal insulin with peak; cloudy suspension; hypoglycemia risk.

Oral antidiabetic; biguanide
Key parameters: decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis, improves insulin sensitivity; weight neutral/loss; GI effects; rare lactic acidosis; avoid severe renal failure.

Oral antidiabetic; sulfonylurea
Key parameters: closes β-cell KATP channels to increase insulin; hypoglycemia and weight gain risk.

Oral antidiabetic; sulfonylurea
Key parameters: insulin secretagogue; lower hypoglycemia risk than some older agents but still possible; weight gain.

Oral antidiabetic; meglitinide/glinide
Key parameters: short-acting insulin secretagogue; taken with meals; hypoglycemia/weight gain possible.

Oral antidiabetic; thiazolidinedione (TZD)
Key parameters: PPARγ agonist; improves insulin sensitivity; adverse effects: edema, weight gain, heart failure worsening, fractures.

Oral antidiabetic; α-glucosidase inhibitor
Key parameters: delays carbohydrate absorption; lowers postprandial glucose; GI adverse effects: flatulence/diarrhea.

Antidiabetic/weight-loss drug; GLP-1 receptor agonist
Key parameters: increases glucose-dependent insulin, slows gastric emptying, reduces appetite; weight loss; GI effects; pancreatitis warning.

Oral antidiabetic; DPP-4 inhibitor
Key parameters: increases endogenous incretins; weight neutral; low hypoglycemia alone; pancreatitis warning.

Oral antidiabetic; SGLT2 inhibitor
Key parameters: glucosuria; cardiovascular/renal benefits in selected patients; adverse effects: genital infections, dehydration, euglycemic ketoacidosis.

Thyroid hormone replacement; synthetic T4
Key parameters: hypothyroidism; long half-life; overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms; absorption affected by calcium/iron.

Antithyroid drug; thionamide
Key parameters: inhibits thyroid peroxidase; hyperthyroidism; adverse effects: agranulocytosis, rash, hepatotoxicity; avoid early pregnancy if possible.

Antithyroid drug; thionamide
Key parameters: inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4→T3 conversion; preferred in thyroid storm/early pregnancy; hepatotoxicity risk.

Glucocorticoid
Key parameters: anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive; adverse effects: Cushingoid features, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, infection risk.

Glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid activity
Key parameters: adrenal insufficiency replacement; stress dosing; shorter acting.

Potent long-acting glucocorticoid
Key parameters: minimal mineralocorticoid activity; cerebral edema, antiemetic, inflammation; adrenal suppression risk.

Mineralocorticoid
Key parameters: aldosterone-like; used in adrenal insufficiency/orthostatic hypotension; adverse effects: hypertension, edema, hypokalemia.

Gout drug; xanthine oxidase inhibitor
Key parameters: lowers uric acid production; chronic gout prophylaxis; hypersensitivity risk; interacts with azathioprine/6-MP.

Gout drug; microtubule inhibitor
Key parameters: acute gout/prophylaxis; inhibits neutrophil migration; adverse effects: diarrhea, myopathy, marrow suppression.

Osteoporosis drug; bisphosphonate
Key parameters: inhibits osteoclasts; take upright with water; adverse effects: esophagitis, osteonecrosis of jaw rare.

Vitamin D supplement
Key parameters: calcium/phosphate homeostasis; deficiency/osteoporosis support; toxicity causes hypercalcemia.

Estrogen hormone
Key parameters: contraception/HRT components; adverse effects: thromboembolism risk, breast/endometrial stimulation depending context.

Antiestrogen/SERM
Key parameters: estrogen antagonist in breast, partial agonist in bone/endometrium; breast cancer; risks: VTE, endometrial cancer.

Immunosuppressant; calcineurin inhibitor
Key parameters: inhibits IL-2 transcription; transplant/autoimmune disease; adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, gingival hyperplasia.

Immunosuppressant; calcineurin inhibitor
Key parameters: inhibits IL-2; transplant; nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, diabetes risk.

Antimetabolite anticancer/immunosuppressant; folate antagonist
Key parameters: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; cancer, RA, psoriasis; adverse effects: myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity; rescue: folinic acid.

Immunosuppressant; purine analogue prodrug
Key parameters: metabolized to 6-MP; transplant/autoimmune disease; myelosuppression; interaction with allopurinol.

Biologic immunosuppressant; anti-TNF monoclonal antibody
Key parameters: chimeric mAb; RA/IBD/psoriasis; infection/TB reactivation risk; infusion reactions.

Biologic immunosuppressant; TNF receptor fusion protein
Key parameters: binds TNF; RA/psoriasis; infection/TB risk.

Immunomodulator/cytokine
Key parameters: antiviral/anticancer uses; flu-like symptoms, depression, myelosuppression.

Anticancer alkylating agent; nitrogen mustard
Key parameters: crosslinks DNA; adverse effects: myelosuppression, hemorrhagic cystitis; prevent cystitis with mesna/hydration.

Anticancer platinum compound
Key parameters: DNA crosslinking; adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuropathy, severe nausea.

Anticancer antimetabolite; pyrimidine analogue
Key parameters: inhibits thymidylate synthase; adverse effects: myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome.

Anticancer cytotoxic antibiotic; anthracycline
Key parameters: intercalates DNA, topoisomerase II inhibition, free radicals; cardiotoxicity; dexrazoxane may protect heart.

Anticancer mitotic poison; vinca alkaloid
Key parameters: inhibits microtubule polymerization; M phase; adverse effect: peripheral neuropathy, constipation; little myelosuppression.

Anticancer mitotic poison; taxane
Key parameters: stabilizes microtubules; M phase; adverse effects: neuropathy, myelosuppression, hypersensitivity.

Targeted anticancer/immunologic drug; anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody
Key parameters: B-cell malignancies/autoimmune disease; infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation, PML rare.

Targeted anticancer drug; anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody
Key parameters: HER2-positive breast/gastric cancer; cardiotoxicity risk; monitor cardiac function.

Targeted anticancer drug; tyrosine kinase inhibitor
Key parameters: BCR-ABL, c-KIT, PDGFR inhibitor; CML/GIST; adverse effects: edema, nausea, myelosuppression.

Cancer immunotherapy; immune checkpoint inhibitor, anti-PD-1 mAb
Key parameters: enhances T-cell response; immune-related adverse effects: colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, endocrinopathies.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class 0 = automaticity/HCN channel blockers
Key parameters: target pacemaker funny current (If) in SA node; prototype: ivabradine; lowers sinus rate without strong negative inotropy; useful for inappropriate sinus tachycardia/selected heart failure patients, but not for acute arrhythmia conversion.

Antiarrhythmic/heart-rate lowering drug; Class 0 HCN/If channel blocker
Key parameters: blocks funny current in SA node; reduces heart rate; requires sinus rhythm; adverse effects: bradycardia, luminous visual phenomena/phosphenes, atrial fibrillation risk.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class I = fast sodium-channel blockers
Key parameters: mainly act on phase 0 depolarization in atrial/ventricular myocardium and Purkinje fibers; subdivided into IA, IB, IC; main danger is proarrhythmia and worsening conduction/contractility.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class IA sodium-channel blockers
Key parameters: moderate Na+ block plus K+ block; prolong action potential duration and QT interval; examples: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide; risks: torsades de pointes, hypotension, anticholinergic effects depending drug.

Antiarrhythmic class IA; sodium-channel blocker with potassium-channel blocking effect
Key parameters: prolongs action potential and QT; can treat atrial and ventricular arrhythmias but limited by toxicity; adverse effects: cinchonism, diarrhea, thrombocytopenia, torsades de pointes.

Antiarrhythmic class IA; sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: prolongs action potential and QT; used for selected supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias; adverse effects: drug-induced lupus, hypotension, torsades de pointes.

Antiarrhythmic class IA; sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: prolongs action potential and QT; strong anticholinergic and negative inotropic effects; avoid/warn in heart failure, glaucoma, urinary retention.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class IB sodium-channel blockers
Key parameters: weak Na+ block; shorten action potential duration; prefer ischemic/depolarized ventricular tissue; examples: lidocaine, mexiletine, phenytoin; used mainly for ventricular arrhythmias.

Antiarrhythmic class IB; oral sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: oral lidocaine-like drug; used for ventricular arrhythmias and some channelopathies; adverse effects: GI upset, tremor, dizziness.

Antiarrhythmic class IB sodium-channel blocker; also antiepileptic
Key parameters: may be used for digoxin-induced ventricular arrhythmias in selected settings; adverse effects include ataxia, nystagmus, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, teratogenicity.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class IC sodium-channel blockers
Key parameters: strong Na+ block; markedly slow conduction; little effect on action potential duration; examples: flecainide, propafenone; avoid in structural heart disease or post-MI because of proarrhythmia risk.

Antiarrhythmic class IC; strong sodium-channel blocker
Key parameters: rhythm control in selected atrial arrhythmias without structural heart disease; can widen QRS; risk of dangerous proarrhythmia, especially in ischemic/structural heart disease.

Antiarrhythmic class IC; strong sodium-channel blocker with beta-blocking activity
Key parameters: rhythm control in selected atrial arrhythmias without structural heart disease; avoid in significant structural heart disease; adverse effects: metallic taste, dizziness, QRS widening, proarrhythmia.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class II = beta-blockers / anti-sympathetic drugs
Key parameters: reduce β1-mediated cAMP effects; slow SA node automaticity and AV node conduction; useful in rate control, SVT prevention, post-MI protection; adverse effects: bradycardia, AV block, bronchospasm with non-selective agents.

Antiarrhythmic class II; ultra-short-acting β1-selective beta-blocker
Key parameters: IV; rapid onset and very short half-life; useful for acute rate control and perioperative tachyarrhythmias; adverse effects: bradycardia, hypotension, AV block.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class III = potassium-channel blockers
Key parameters: prolong repolarization and effective refractory period; prolong QT interval; examples: amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide, dronedarone; main danger: torsades de pointes, except amiodarone has lower torsades risk but many organ toxicities.

Antiarrhythmic class III with class II beta-blocking activity
Key parameters: blocks K+ channels and β receptors; used for selected atrial and ventricular arrhythmias; adverse effects: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, bradycardia, bronchospasm risk.

Antiarrhythmic class III; potassium-channel blocker
Key parameters: rhythm control in atrial fibrillation/flutter in selected patients; requires QT and renal monitoring; major risk: torsades de pointes.

Antiarrhythmic class III; potassium-channel blocker
Key parameters: IV conversion of atrial flutter/fibrillation in selected settings; major risk: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.

Antiarrhythmic class III; amiodarone analogue
Key parameters: rhythm control in selected atrial fibrillation patients; less iodine-related toxicity than amiodarone but less effective; contraindicated in severe/decompensated heart failure and permanent AF.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class IV = non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers
Key parameters: verapamil and diltiazem; slow AV node conduction and reduce heart rate; useful for SVT and AF rate control; adverse effects: bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, constipation especially verapamil.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class V = miscellaneous antiarrhythmics
Key parameters: drugs that do not fit cleanly into Classes I-IV; examples: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium sulfate, atropine; mechanisms vary, because apparently one tidy classification was too merciful.

Antiarrhythmic class V; endogenous nucleoside
Key parameters: transiently blocks AV nodal conduction via A1 receptors; first-line acute termination of many regular narrow-complex SVTs; very short half-life; adverse effects: flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnea, brief asystole feeling.

Antiarrhythmic class V; electrolyte therapy
Key parameters: treatment of torsades de pointes and arrhythmias related to hypomagnesemia; also used in eclampsia; adverse effects: hypotension, flushing, loss of reflexes/respiratory depression in toxicity.

Antiarrhythmic class V use; antimuscarinic vagolytic
Key parameters: blocks muscarinic receptors and increases SA/AV node activity; used for symptomatic bradycardia; adverse effects: tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion.

Antiarrhythmic class V use; cardiac glycoside with vagotonic AV-node effect
Key parameters: slows AV nodal conduction and helps rate control in atrial fibrillation, especially with heart failure; narrow therapeutic index; toxicity causes arrhythmias, GI symptoms, visual disturbances.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class VI = connexin/gap-junction modifiers
Key parameters: target cell-to-cell electrical coupling through connexins; mostly experimental or not routine clinical antiarrhythmics; example concept: gap-junction enhancers such as rotigaptide; exam note: know the target more than a standard drug list.

Experimental antiarrhythmic concept; Class VI connexin/gap-junction enhancer
Key parameters: investigational gap-junction modifier; aims to improve intercellular conduction and reduce re-entry substrate; not a routine clinical antiarrhythmic.

Antiarrhythmic classification; Class VII = upstream/remodeling-target drugs
Key parameters: target long-term arrhythmogenic remodeling rather than acute ion-channel blockade; examples often include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, statins, and anti-inflammatory/antifibrotic approaches; clinically relevant as prevention/support, not acute conversion.

Antiarrhythmic concept; Class VII remodeling prevention
Key parameters: reduces atrial/ventricular remodeling drivers such as fibrosis, stretch, inflammation, and neurohormonal activation; examples: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, aldosterone antagonists, statins in selected contexts; supportive rather than classic acute antiarrhythmic therapy.

Heart failure drug class; ARB + neprilysin inhibitor combination
Key parameters: combines RAAS blockade with increased natriuretic peptides; prototype is sacubitril/valsartan; used especially in chronic HFrEF; adverse effects: hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal function worsening, angioedema risk.

ARNI; angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
Key parameters: sacubitril inhibits neprilysin and valsartan blocks AT1 receptors; used in chronic HFrEF to reduce morbidity/mortality; do not combine with ACE inhibitors; requires ACE inhibitor washout because of angioedema risk.

Neprilysin inhibitor component of ARNI
Key parameters: increases natriuretic peptides by inhibiting their breakdown; promotes natriuresis, vasodilation, and reduced remodeling signals; clinically used only in fixed combination with valsartan.

Heart failure safety card
Key parameters: contraindicated with ACE inhibitors, pregnancy, history of angioedema related to ACEi/ARB/ARNI, and significant hyperkalemia; caution in renal impairment, hypotension, and bilateral renal artery stenosis.

front: SGLT2 inhibitors in chronic heart failure
back:
Heart failure drug class; sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
Key parameters: reduce heart failure hospitalization and improve outcomes in HFrEF and many HFpEF patients; mechanisms include osmotic diuresis, natriuresis, renal/metabolic benefits; adverse effects: genital infections, volume depletion, euglycemic ketoacidosis risk.

SGLT2 inhibitor; heart failure and antidiabetic drug
Key parameters: promotes glucosuria and natriuresis; used in diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and chronic heart failure; adverse effects: genital mycotic infections, dehydration, hypotension, euglycemic ketoacidosis.

SGLT2 inhibitor; heart failure disease-modifying drug
Key parameters: useful in chronic heart failure even without diabetes; causes glucosuria/natriuresis; adverse effects: genital infections, volume depletion, rare euglycemic ketoacidosis.

front: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in heart failure
back:
Heart failure drug class; aldosterone receptor blockers
Key parameters: reduce aldosterone-mediated sodium retention, potassium loss, fibrosis, and remodeling; examples: spironolactone, eplerenone; adverse effect: hyperkalemia; monitor renal function and potassium.

Potassium-sparing diuretic; selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
Key parameters: used in HFrEF and post-MI LV dysfunction; less gynecomastia than spironolactone; adverse effects: hyperkalemia, renal function worsening.

Heart failure vasodilator combination
Key parameters: hydralazine reduces afterload and isosorbide dinitrate reduces preload; option in HFrEF when ACEi/ARB/ARNI not tolerated or as add-on in selected patients; adverse effects: headache, hypotension, reflex tachycardia.

Organic nitrate; antianginal and heart failure preload reducer
Key parameters: releases NO and increases cGMP; venodilation reduces preload; used in angina and with hydralazine in selected HFrEF; adverse effects: headache, hypotension, tolerance; contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.

Direct arterial vasodilator; antihypertensive/heart failure add-on
Key parameters: relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle and lowers afterload; used in pregnancy hypertension, hypertensive urgency/emergency in selected cases, and with nitrates in HFrEF; adverse effects: reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, headache, drug-induced lupus.

front: Central alpha-2 agonists and imidazoline agonists
back:
Centrally acting antihypertensive class
Key parameters: reduce sympathetic outflow from the CNS; examples: clonidine, methyldopa, moxonidine; adverse effects: sedation, dry mouth, bradycardia; clonidine withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension.

Central α2-adrenergic agonist; antihypertensive
Key parameters: decreases sympathetic outflow; used in resistant hypertension and some withdrawal syndromes; adverse effects: sedation, dry mouth, bradycardia, rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly.

Central α2-adrenergic agonist; antihypertensive
Key parameters: classic antihypertensive in pregnancy; converted to α-methylnoradrenaline; adverse effects: sedation, hyperprolactinemia, hemolytic anemia, hepatotoxicity.

Imidazoline I1 receptor agonist; centrally acting antihypertensive
Key parameters: reduces sympathetic tone; used in hypertension in some settings; adverse effects: dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, bradycardia.

Antihypertensive class; vascular smooth muscle relaxants
Key parameters: reduce systemic vascular resistance by arteriolar dilation; examples: hydralazine and minoxidil; adverse effects: reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, so often combined with beta-blocker/diuretic when appropriate.

Direct arterial vasodilator; K+ channel opener
Key parameters: potent antihypertensive for resistant hypertension; also used topically for alopecia; adverse effects: fluid retention, reflex tachycardia, hypertrichosis, pericardial effusion rarely.

Acute blood pressure control class; mainly IV agents
Key parameters: used for severe hypertension with acute target-organ damage; reduce BP in a controlled way; examples: labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, urapidil; choice depends on clinical scenario.

Beta-blocker with α1-blocking activity; IV/oral antihypertensive
Key parameters: blocks β1/β2 and α1 receptors; useful in hypertensive emergency and pregnancy-related severe hypertension; adverse effects: hypotension, bradycardia, bronchospasm risk.

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker; IV antihypertensive
Key parameters: arterial vasodilator used in hypertensive emergency and neurologic BP control; adverse effects: headache, flushing, reflex tachycardia, edema.

Antihypertensive; α1 antagonist with central serotonergic sympatholytic effect
Key parameters: IV option for hypertensive crisis in some countries; lowers peripheral resistance with less reflex tachycardia; adverse effects: dizziness, headache, hypotension.

Antiplatelet class; ADP receptor antagonists
Key parameters: inhibit platelet activation through P2Y12 blockade; examples: clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor; used in ACS and after stenting; major adverse effect: bleeding.

Antiplatelet drug; irreversible P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist
Key parameters: prodrug; stronger platelet inhibition than clopidogrel; used in ACS/PCI; adverse effect: bleeding; avoid in prior stroke/TIA.

Antiplatelet drug; reversible P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist
Key parameters: not a prodrug; used in ACS and after stenting; adverse effects: bleeding, dyspnea, bradyarrhythmias; interacts with strong CYP3A modifiers.

Antiplatelet class; final common pathway platelet aggregation blockers
Key parameters: block fibrinogen-mediated platelet cross-linking; examples: abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban; mainly IV use in selected ACS/PCI settings; major risks: bleeding and thrombocytopenia.

GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor; monoclonal antibody fragment antiplatelet
Key parameters: blocks platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors; IV use in selected PCI/ACS settings; adverse effects: bleeding, thrombocytopenia.

GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor; cyclic peptide antiplatelet
Key parameters: IV reversible platelet aggregation inhibitor; used in selected ACS/PCI settings; adverse effects: bleeding, thrombocytopenia; renal dosing matters.

GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor; non-peptide antiplatelet
Key parameters: IV reversible GPIIb/IIIa blocker; selected ACS/PCI use; adverse effects: bleeding, thrombocytopenia; adjust in renal impairment.

Hemostasis/antidote category
Key parameters: reverse or bypass anticoagulant effect in major bleeding or urgent procedures; examples: protamine for heparin, vitamin K/PCC for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors where available.

Antidote; heparin reversal agent
Key parameters: positively charged protein that binds negatively charged heparin; reverses unfractionated heparin best and partially reverses LMWH; adverse effects: hypotension, anaphylactoid reactions.

Antidote; warfarin reversal support
Key parameters: restores hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; used for warfarin over-anticoagulation/bleeding; slow compared with PCC; effect depends on liver synthetic function.

Anticoagulant reversal product; clotting factor concentrate
Key parameters: rapidly replaces vitamin K-dependent factors, especially for serious warfarin-associated bleeding; often combined with vitamin K; major risk: thrombosis.

Antidote; dabigatran reversal monoclonal antibody fragment
Key parameters: binds dabigatran and rapidly reverses direct thrombin inhibition; used for life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery; thrombosis risk after reversal if anticoagulation not restarted when appropriate.

Antidote; factor Xa inhibitor reversal agent
Key parameters: recombinant modified factor Xa decoy; reverses apixaban/rivaroxaban in selected severe bleeding settings where available; adverse effects: thrombosis risk, infusion reactions.

Hypolipidemic drug; cholesterol absorption inhibitor
Key parameters: inhibits NPC1L1 cholesterol uptake in the intestine; lowers LDL; used alone or with statins; adverse effects: GI upset, liver enzyme elevation especially with statins.

Hypolipidemic biologic class; LDL receptor recycling enhancers
Key parameters: monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9 increase hepatic LDL receptor recycling and markedly lower LDL; examples: evolocumab, alirocumab; adverse effects: injection-site reactions, flu-like symptoms.

PCSK9 inhibitor; monoclonal antibody hypolipidemic
Key parameters: greatly lowers LDL by increasing LDL receptor recycling; used in familial hypercholesterolemia or high-risk ASCVD when LDL remains high; adverse effects: injection-site reactions.

PCSK9 inhibitor; monoclonal antibody hypolipidemic
Key parameters: lowers LDL by inhibiting PCSK9; used in high-risk dyslipidemia and familial hypercholesterolemia; adverse effects: injection-site reactions, nasopharyngitis.

Hypolipidemic class; PPAR-α agonists
Key parameters: mainly lower triglycerides and raise HDL modestly; examples: fenofibrate, gemfibrozil; adverse effects: myopathy risk especially with statins, gallstones, liver enzyme elevation.

Fibrate hypolipidemic; PPAR-α agonist
Key parameters: lowers triglycerides by increasing lipoprotein lipase activity; used in hypertriglyceridemia; adverse effects: myopathy, gallstones, liver enzyme elevation.

Hypolipidemic class; intestinal bile acid binders
Key parameters: bind bile acids in gut and increase hepatic LDL receptor expression; examples: cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam; adverse effects: constipation, bloating, reduced absorption of other drugs/vitamins.

Bile acid sequestrant; hypolipidemic resin
Key parameters: lowers LDL by binding bile acids; also useful for some bile acid diarrhea and pruritus from cholestasis; adverse effects: constipation, bloating, drug binding interactions.

front: PDE5 inhibitors in pulmonary arterial hypertension
back:
Pulmonary hypertension vasodilator class
Key parameters: inhibit PDE5 and increase cGMP-mediated pulmonary vasodilation; example: sildenafil; adverse effects: headache, flushing, hypotension; contraindicated with nitrates because of severe hypotension risk.

PDE5 inhibitor; pulmonary arterial hypertension and erectile dysfunction drug
Key parameters: increases cGMP by inhibiting PDE5; causes pulmonary and systemic vasodilation; adverse effects: headache, flushing, hypotension, visual disturbance; contraindicated with nitrates.
Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion; the core pharmacokinetic sequence determining drug concentration over time.
Movement of drug from administration site into blood; affected by route, solubility, pH, blood flow, formulation, food, and transporters.
Fraction of administered dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged; IV is 100%; oral drugs may lose bioavailability through incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.
Presystemic metabolism mainly in gut wall and liver before drug reaches systemic circulation; lowers oral bioavailability.
Enteral: oral, sublingual, rectal. Parenteral: IV, IM, SC, inhaled, transdermal. Route affects onset, bioavailability, and safety.
Movement of drug from blood into tissues; influenced by perfusion, plasma protein binding, lipid solubility, barriers, and volume of distribution.
Apparent volume relating amount of drug in body to plasma concentration; high Vd suggests tissue binding/distribution, low Vd suggests blood/plasma confinement.
Only free drug is pharmacologically active and filtered; displacement interactions matter most for highly bound narrow-therapeutic-index drugs.
Volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time; mainly renal and hepatic; determines maintenance dose.
Time for plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%; determines dosing interval and time to steady state.
Drug input equals elimination; usually reached after about 4-5 half-lives with repeated dosing.
Initial larger dose used to rapidly reach target concentration; depends mainly on volume of distribution and target concentration.
Dose needed to maintain steady-state concentration; depends mainly on clearance, target concentration, dosing interval, and bioavailability.
Safety margin between effective and toxic doses; narrow therapeutic index drugs require monitoring, e.g. warfarin, digoxin, lithium.
Potency = dose needed for effect; efficacy = maximal effect. More potent does not necessarily mean more effective.
Binds receptor and produces maximal response when enough receptors are occupied.
Activates receptor but produces lower maximal response than full agonist; can antagonize a full agonist in the same system.
Reversibly competes with agonist at receptor; effect can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration; shifts dose-response curve right.
Reduces maximal response; effect cannot be fully overcome by increasing agonist concentration.
Augmented, dose-related, predictable from pharmacology; common example: bleeding from anticoagulants.
Bizarre/idiosyncratic or immune-mediated, not clearly dose-related; example: drug allergy or anaphylaxis.
Detection, assessment, understanding, and prevention of adverse drug effects after drugs are marketed.
Interactions affecting absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion; examples: enzyme inhibition/induction, altered renal clearance.
Interactions at effect level without changing concentration; examples: additive CNS depression, additive bleeding risk, antagonistic receptor effects.
Higher risk from reduced renal/hepatic function, polypharmacy, altered body composition, and sensitivity to CNS/anticholinergic drugs; start low, go slow.
Drugs can cause teratogenicity, fetal toxicity, or neonatal toxicity; risk depends on drug, dose, timing, and placental transfer.
A prescription should clearly state patient, drug name, strength, dosage form, route, dose, frequency, duration, quantity, instructions, date, and prescriber.
Positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors; increase frequency of chloride channel opening; anxiolytic, hypnotic, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant.
GABA-A enhancers that prolong chloride channel opening; anticonvulsant/anesthetic uses; dangerous overdose with CNS and respiratory depression.
Hypnotics acting at benzodiazepine site on GABA-A, relatively sleep-selective; examples: zolpidem, zopiclone; used for insomnia.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; first-line for depression/anxiety; adverse effects include GI upset, sexual dysfunction, serotonin syndrome risk.
Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; examples: venlafaxine, duloxetine; used in depression, anxiety, neuropathic pain.
Inhibit serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake; anticholinergic, sedating, and cardiotoxic in overdose; examples: amitriptyline, imipramine.
Increase monoamines by inhibiting monoamine oxidase; risk of hypertensive crisis with tyramine and serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.
Mainly D2 antagonists; useful in psychosis/agitation; adverse effects: extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, QT prolongation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism/partial agonism patterns; lower EPS generally, but more metabolic effects; examples: clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine.
Stabilize inactive Na+ channels and reduce high-frequency neuronal firing; examples: phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine.
Increase inhibitory neurotransmission; examples include benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, valproate, tiagabine, vigabatrin.
Antiepileptics acting on synaptic vesicle protein SV2A; prototype: levetiracetam; few interactions but mood/irritability possible.
Emergency treatment: benzodiazepine first, then loading antiepileptic such as levetiracetam/phenytoin/valproate; refractory cases may need anesthetic coma.
Mu-opioid receptor agonists causing analgesia, sedation, miosis, respiratory depression, constipation, tolerance, and dependence; overdose antidote: naloxone.
Block opioid receptors; naloxone reverses overdose acutely, naltrexone is longer acting and used in dependence treatment.
Inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce prostaglandins; analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory; adverse effects: GI bleeding, renal injury, bronchospasm, CV risk.
Toxic metabolite depletes glutathione and causes hepatic necrosis; antidote is N-acetylcysteine, best early but useful later too.
Produce reversible unconsciousness/amnesia/immobility; examples: propofol, ketamine, sevoflurane; risks include hypotension, respiratory depression, malignant hyperthermia with volatile agents.
Block voltage-gated sodium channels; prevent nerve impulse conduction; toxicity includes CNS symptoms, seizures, arrhythmias; severe toxicity treated with lipid emulsion.
Causes bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, bronchospasm, hypoglycemia; treatment may include atropine, glucagon, vasopressors, high-dose insulin therapy.
Causes hypotension, bradycardia/AV block especially verapamil/diltiazem, hyperglycemia; treatment includes calcium, vasopressors, high-dose insulin-glucose therapy.
Symptoms: GI upset, confusion, visual changes, arrhythmias, hyperkalemia in acute poisoning; severe toxicity treated with digoxin immune Fab.
CNS excitation/seizures followed by cardiovascular collapse; treat with airway support, benzodiazepines for seizures, and IV lipid emulsion.
Blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase causing cellular hypoxia and lactic acidosis; antidote: hydroxocobalamin.
Oxidized hemoglobin cannot carry oxygen effectively; cyanosis with low pulse oximetry; antidote: methylene blue.
Causes GI corrosion, shock, metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure; antidote/chelator: deferoxamine.
Inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding PBPs; bactericidal; main groups: penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams.
Penicillin G/V; good for many Gram-positive organisms and spirochetes; beta-lactamase sensitive; allergy risk.
Amoxicillin/ampicillin; broader Gram-negative coverage than penicillin G; often combined with beta-lactamase inhibitor.
Oxacillin/flucloxacillin/nafcillin; beta-lactamase-resistant; used for MSSA, not MRSA.
Piperacillin/ticarcillin; cover Pseudomonas; usually combined with tazobactam/clavulanate in severe infections.
Clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam; inhibit many beta-lactamases and expand beta-lactam spectrum; little antibacterial activity alone.
1st gen mainly Gram-positive; later generations add Gram-negative/CNS coverage; cefepime covers Pseudomonas; ceftaroline covers MRSA.
Very broad beta-lactams; examples: meropenem, imipenem; severe resistant infections; seizure risk especially imipenem.
Aztreonam; active against aerobic Gram-negative rods including Pseudomonas; minimal cross-allergy with penicillins.
Glycopeptide inhibiting cell wall synthesis; used for MRSA and severe Gram-positive infections; adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, red man syndrome.
Oxazolidinone inhibiting 50S initiation complex; active against MRSA/VRE; adverse effects: thrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome risk.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; blocks folate synthesis sequentially; uses include UTI, Pneumocystis jirovecii, some MRSA; adverse effects include rash, marrow suppression, hyperkalemia.
Urinary antiseptic for uncomplicated lower UTI; not for pyelonephritis; adverse effects include GI upset, pulmonary toxicity rarely, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
50S protein synthesis inhibitors; cover atypical respiratory pathogens; examples: azithromycin, clarithromycin; adverse effects: QT prolongation, GI upset.
30S inhibitors; examples: doxycycline; cover atypicals, rickettsiae, chlamydia, acne; adverse effects: photosensitivity, teeth/bone effects; avoid pregnancy/children.
30S inhibitors with concentration-dependent killing; Gram-negative aerobes; adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade.
Inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase; adverse effects: tendinopathy, QT prolongation, CNS effects, dysglycemia; avoid pregnancy/children if possible.
Acyclovir/valacyclovir; guanosine analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase; inhibit viral DNA polymerase; HSV/VZV; nephrotoxicity risk.
Main classes: NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors, entry/fusion inhibitors; usually combined to prevent resistance.
Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors; backbone of many HIV regimens; examples: tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavir.
Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; examples: efavirenz, nevirapine, rilpivirine; rash and CYP interactions are important.
Prevent viral protein processing; examples: ritonavir, darunavir; adverse effects: metabolic syndrome, lipodystrophy, many CYP interactions.
Block HIV integration into host genome; examples: dolutegravir, raltegravir, bictegravir; generally well tolerated.
HBV: tenofovir, entecavir. HCV: direct-acting antivirals such as sofosbuvir-based regimens.
Inhibit ergosterol synthesis via 14-alpha-demethylase; examples: fluconazole, voriconazole; adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, CYP interactions.
Inhibit fungal beta-glucan cell wall synthesis; examples: caspofungin, micafungin; useful for Candida including invasive disease.
Chloroquine for sensitive malaria, artemisinin combinations for many falciparum cases, primaquine for hypnozoites; resistance and region matter.
Antimalarial active against sensitive Plasmodium; also rheumatologic use; adverse effects: retinopathy, QT prolongation, pruritus.
Rapidly acting antimalarials used in combination therapy for falciparum malaria; adverse effects include GI symptoms and rare QT issues depending partner drug.
Kills dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax/ovale; can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; test G6PD before use.
Rapid bronchodilators for symptoms; main prototype is salbutamol; formoterol can be used as reliever in ICS-formoterol regimens.
Reduce airway inflammation and exacerbations; inhaled corticosteroids are the core controllers; LABA/LAMA/leukotriene antagonists are add-ons.
Long-acting beta2 agonists such as salmeterol and formoterol; maintenance therapy in asthma/COPD; in asthma should be used with inhaled corticosteroid.
Budesonide/fluticasone; first-line anti-inflammatory controllers in persistent asthma; adverse effects: oral candidiasis, dysphonia.
Leukotriene receptor antagonist; used in asthma/allergic rhinitis; less effective than inhaled corticosteroids; neuropsychiatric adverse effects possible.
Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody for severe allergic asthma/urticaria; reduces allergic inflammation; injection reactions/anaphylaxis rare.
Suppress cough; examples: codeine, dextromethorphan; use mainly for dry irritating cough; avoid suppressing productive dangerous cough unnecessarily.
Reduce mucus viscosity or aid clearance; examples: acetylcysteine, ambroxol, guaifenesin.
Block gastric H2 receptors and reduce acid secretion; example: famotidine; useful in GERD/ulcer disease though PPIs are stronger.
H2 receptor antagonist; reduces gastric acid secretion; fewer CYP interactions than cimetidine.
Mucosal protectant forming a protective barrier over ulcers; requires acidic pH; can reduce absorption of other drugs.
Usually PPI plus antibiotics such as amoxicillin/clarithromycin/metronidazole depending local resistance; improves peptic ulcer cure and recurrence.
Bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, and stool-softening agents; examples: psyllium, lactulose/macrogol, senna/bisacodyl, docusate.
5-ASA for mild ulcerative colitis, corticosteroids for flares, immunosuppressants/biologics for maintenance or severe disease.
Rapid: lispro/aspart; short: regular; intermediate: NPH; long: glargine/detemir/degludec. Main risks: hypoglycemia and weight gain.
Main groups: metformin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, TZDs, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists.
Close beta-cell KATP channels and increase insulin release; examples: gliclazide, glibenclamide; adverse effects: hypoglycemia, weight gain.
Short-acting insulin secretagogues taken with meals; example: repaglinide; risk of hypoglycemia and weight gain.
PPAR-gamma agonists improving insulin sensitivity; example: pioglitazone; adverse effects: edema, weight gain, heart failure worsening, fractures.
Delay carbohydrate absorption in intestine; example: acarbose; adverse effects: flatulence, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort.
Increase glucose-dependent insulin, slow gastric emptying, reduce appetite; examples: semaglutide, liraglutide; weight loss and GI effects.
Increase endogenous incretins; examples: sitagliptin, linagliptin; weight neutral, low hypoglycemia alone, pancreatitis warning.
Increase urinary glucose excretion; examples: empagliflozin, dapagliflozin; benefits in selected CV/renal/HF patients; risks: genital infections, dehydration, euglycemic ketoacidosis.
Levothyroxine is synthetic T4 for hypothyroidism; long half-life; absorption reduced by iron/calcium; overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms.
Methimazole and propylthiouracil inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis; adverse effects: agranulocytosis, rash, hepatotoxicity.
Emergency: beta-blocker, thionamide, iodine after thionamide, glucocorticoid, supportive care; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.
Estrogen + progestin suppress ovulation; adverse effects: nausea, breast tenderness, VTE risk; contraindicated in high-risk thrombotic states.
Thickens cervical mucus and may suppress ovulation; useful when estrogen is contraindicated; irregular bleeding common.
SERM that blocks estrogen feedback at hypothalamus, increasing GnRH/FSH/LH; used for ovulation induction.
Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive drugs; adverse effects: Cushingoid features, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection risk, adrenal suppression.
Inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; examples: alendronate, zoledronate; adverse effects: esophagitis, osteonecrosis of jaw rare.
Monoclonal antibody against RANKL; reduces osteoclast formation; osteoporosis treatment; risks: hypocalcemia, infections, rebound fractures if stopped abruptly.
NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids; choice depends on renal function, GI risk, interactions, and contraindications.
Urate-lowering therapy such as allopurinol/febuxostat; start with flare prophylaxis; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase.
Main cytotoxic groups: alkylating agents, platinum compounds, antimetabolites, mitotic inhibitors, cytotoxic antibiotics/topoisomerase inhibitors.
Crosslink DNA; example: cyclophosphamide; adverse effects: myelosuppression, infertility, hemorrhagic cystitis prevented by mesna/hydration.
Cisplatin/carboplatin/oxaliplatin crosslink DNA; toxicities include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuropathy, severe nausea, myelosuppression depending drug.
Interfere with DNA/RNA synthesis; examples: methotrexate, 5-FU, cytarabine; adverse effects: myelosuppression, mucositis.
Vinca alkaloids inhibit microtubule polymerization; taxanes stabilize microtubules; main toxicities: neuropathy and myelosuppression depending drug.
Doxorubicin/daunorubicin intercalate DNA and inhibit topoisomerase II; major dose-limiting toxicity: cardiomyopathy; dexrazoxane may protect.
Cyclosporine and tacrolimus inhibit IL-2 transcription; transplant/autoimmune use; adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, neurotoxicity.
Immunosuppressant inhibiting inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and lymphocyte purine synthesis; adverse effects: GI upset, myelosuppression, teratogenicity.
-mab drugs are monoclonal antibodies; target selection determines use/toxicity, e.g. rituximab anti-CD20, trastuzumab anti-HER2, infliximab anti-TNF.
Anti-PD-1/PD-L1/CTLA-4 drugs enhance antitumor immunity; adverse effects are immune-related: colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, endocrinopathies.
Biologic immunosuppressants for RA/IBD/psoriasis; examples: infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept; screen for TB; infection risk.
Pooled immunoglobulin used for immune deficiencies and autoimmune diseases; adverse effects: infusion reactions, thrombosis, renal dysfunction rarely.
Cytokine immunomodulators used in some viral/malignant/immune diseases; adverse effects: flu-like symptoms, depression, myelosuppression.
